lines.content: PlayStation -1 is a lightweight collection of keyboard-driven command-line games for quick breaks in the terminal. The project keeps the experience simple: choose a game, play without leaving the shell, and return to the menu when you are finished.
The minimum viable product contains one Wordle-style word-guessing game. Players receive feedback after each guess and can complete a short game session entirely from the command line.
Prerequisites: JDK 25 (use the exact version), update Intellij to the most recent version.

1. **Ensure Intellij JDK 25 is defined as an SDK**, as described [here](https://www.jetbrains.com/help/idea/sdk.html#set-up-jdk) -- this step is not needed if you have used JDK 25 in a previous Intellij project.
1. **Import the project _as a Gradle project_**, as described [here](https://se-education.org/guides/tutorials/intellijImportGradleProject.html).

1. **Verify the setup**: After importing, run the application from IntelliJ or execute `./gradlew run` (macOS/Linux) or `gradlew.bat run` (Windows) in the project folder. A successful run starts the command-line application.

**Warning:** Keep the `src\main\java` folder as the root folder for Java files (i.e., don't rename those folders or move Java files to another folder outside of this folder path), as this is the default location some tools (e.g., Gradle) expect to find Java files.
* This project uses Gradle for build automation and dependency management. It includes a basic build script as well (i.e. the `build.gradle` file).
* If you are new to Gradle, refer to the [Gradle Tutorial at se-education.org/guides](https://se-education.org/guides/tutorials/gradle.html).
* To run _I/O redirection_ tests (aka _Text UI tests_), navigate to the `text-ui-test` and run the `runtest(.bat/.sh)` script.
* Run the JUnit test suite with `./gradlew test` (macOS/Linux) or `gradlew.bat test` (Windows).
* If you are new to JUnit, refer to the [JUnit Tutorial at se-education.org/guides](https://se-education.org/guides/tutorials/junit.html).
* A sample CheckStyle rule configuration is provided in this project.
* If you are new to Checkstyle, refer to the [Checkstyle Tutorial at se-education.org/guides](https://se-education.org/guides/tutorials/checkstyle.html).

The app reads one line at a time. `PlayStationMinusOne` owns the input loop; `CommandHandler` routes launcher commands and active-game input; `GameList` looks up games by ID; and `Ui` prints responses. Each game implements the shared `Game` interface.

The `CommandHandler` refactor moved command routing and active-game state out of the application entry point. It parses launcher commands, selects a game for `play <gameId>`, forwards other input unchanged, and resets a game after it finishes.
![Sequence diagram showing how a game is selected](diagrams/command-routing.png)

`WordleGame` implements `Game` as game ID `1`. It selects one answer from the bundled word list for each session. Guesses must contain five letters; malformed or repeated guesses do not use a try. `WordleHelp` provides coloured feedback and tracks hints for `list letters`.

`BattleshipGame` implements `Game` as game ID `3`. It manages a turn-based game against the computer. Each participant has a 7 × 7 board containing four randomly placed ships of lengths 4, 3, 2 and 1. `BattleshipBoard` handles ship placement and attacks, while `Cell` and `Ship` track occupied positions and damage. `ShotResult` reports a miss, hit, or sunk ship. Invalid or repeated coordinates do not consume a turn. The computer draws its attacks from a shuffled list to avoid repeated shots.
### Tic Tac Toe enhancement (Lim Zi Jing)

Tic Tac Toe is game ID `4`. The player uses `X`; the computer uses `O`. `TicTacToeGame` manages turns and session messages, while `TicTacToeBoard` stores the 3-by-3 grid and checks moves and outcomes. This separation keeps board rules in one class and turn flow in another.

A move is entered as a coordinate from `A1` to `C3`. Invalid or occupied squares leave the board unchanged and do not trigger a computer move. After a valid `X` move, the game checks for a win or draw. If the game continues, it chooses randomly from the remaining empty squares, places `O`, and checks the result again. The game shows the updated board and returns to the menu when the session ends.
![Sequence diagram of a normal Tic Tac Toe turn](diagrams/tictactoe-turn-sequence.png)
The computer chooses from a list of empty squares, so it cannot overwrite a mark. `TicTacToeGame` accepts an injected `Random` source, which lets tests make its moves repeatable.

GTA -6 is game ID `5`, a choose-your-own-adventure game. The player navigates a branching story by picking numbered choices. The story is modelled as a graph of `StoryNode` objects stored in a `Map<String, StoryNode>`. Each `StoryNode` holds scenario text, choice labels, and keys pointing to the next nodes. Ending nodes have no choices and finish the session.

When the player enters a choice number, `GtaGame.handleInput()` looks up the current node's choice keys, advances to the next node, and returns its formatted text. If the next node is an ending, the game sets itself as finished. Invalid input re-displays the current scenario without advancing.

## Appendix E: Instructions for Manual Testing
1. Start the app and enter `list`; confirm Tic Tac Toe appears as game ID `4`.
2. Enter `play 4`; confirm the instructions and empty board appear.
3. Enter an invalid coordinate such as `Z9`, then an occupied square; confirm neither causes a computer move.
4. Enter valid coordinates until the game ends; confirm the result and updated board appear.
5. Enter `play 4` again; confirm the board is empty for the new session.

PlayStation -1 is a keyboard-first command-line arcade for people who enjoy quick, self-contained games without leaving the terminal. It is designed for short breaks: start a game with one command, play for as long as you like, and return to the menu when you are done.

Version 1.0 provides a terminal menu and a data-driven game catalogue featuring the **calculator** game. Players can view help and game information, launch the game, solve randomly generated arithmetic problems, receive immediate feedback, and see a session summary when they quit. All interaction is through the keyboard, and scores last for the current session only.

PlayStation -1 is a collection of small games that you play by typing in a terminal. It is made for people who spend their day at a command line and want a short break that has a clear end, without opening a graphical game. Each game finishes in a few minutes, and you can leave any game at any time.
- Implemented a complete turn-based Battleship game where players compete against a computer on a 7 × 7 grid.
- Designed the game using `BattleshipGame`, `BattleshipBoard`, `Ship`, and `Cell` classes.
- Implemented random ship placement, attack validation, hit detection, and win/loss conditions.
- Developed a computer opponent that attacks randomly without repeating coordinates.
- Implemented session statistics, including rounds played, hits, misses, and accuracy.
- Added game reset functionality to support replayability.
- Handled edge cases such as invalid coordinates and repeated attacks without consuming turns.
**Technical challenges:** Ensuring consistent game state across multiple classes while coordinating player and computer turns, tracking ship damage, and handling game-ending conditions.
* Documented the **[Game: Battleship](UserGuide.md#game-battleship)** section, including the game's objective, rules and coordinate input format.
* Explained the `board` command and the meanings of `S`, `O`, `X` and `~`.
* Added sample player-facing outputs, invalid/repeated input behaviour, game-ending conditions and session statistics.

* Documented the **[Battleship game](DeveloperGuide.md#battleship-game-enhancement)** design and implementation, including class responsibilities, random ship placement, turn handling, computer target selection, game state and trade-offs.
